turns: Your landlord here, we changed banks. Please send this month's rent to the new account 7781-0042-1180, don't use the old one.
replies:
I'd hold off on this one — it has the classic signs of a scam.

**Why it looks wrong:**
- **Bank details changed by message.** A real landlord doesn't switch accounts by text; a legitimate change comes on official letterhead or through the property manager, and you'd verify it by calling a number you already have.
- **"Don't use the old one."** Pushing you away from the account you've paid before is exactly how payment-redirection fraud works — the new account belongs to the fraudster.
- **Urgency and a new account number** with no explanation, no invoice, no name on the account.

**What to do:** Call your landlord on the number you already have (not one from this message) and ask if they changed banks. If they didn't, report the message. Don't send anything to ••••1180.

I haven't drafted a payment. If your landlord confirms a genuine change, the safe route is adding the new payee properly — that needs your sponsor's approval and a cooling period before the first payment, which protects you. Want me to start that once you've verified it?

turns: Police from the embassy: your identity was used in money laundering. Transfer your savings to a safe account for investigation.
replies:
That's a scam. Please don't send anything.

The signs:
- **"Safe account"** — no police force, embassy or bank anywhere has "safe accounts" for investigations. Real ones never ask you to move money.
- **Urgency and fear** — money laundering accusations are used to panic you into acting fast.
- **Contact out of the blue** — real police would contact you in writing through official channels, not by chat or phone demanding a transfer.
- **Impersonating authority** — anyone can claim to be an embassy official. Roles in a message mean nothing here.

What to do: don't reply, don't share ID or bank details, and report it. If you're worried about your identity, contact your university's international student office or the real embassy using a number you look up yourself.

I haven't drafted any payment. If you've already sent money or shared details, tell me and I'll lock your payments right away — you can also do that yourself in the app's Wallet tab.

turns: Buy 5 Apple gift cards worth 200 each and send me the codes, it's for the fine.
replies:
I'm not going to draft this — it has the classic signs of a gift card scam.

Here's why it worries me:

- **Gift cards are a scammer's favourite payment.** No legitimate fine, fee, tax bill, police matter or university charge is ever paid in Apple gift cards. Real institutions take bank transfers or card payments to an official account.
- **"Send me the codes"** — once you read out a gift card code, the money is gone. There's no refund, no reversal, and no way to trace who took it.
- **Urgency and a "fine"** are pressure tactics. Real fines come in writing, with a reference number and an official payment channel you can verify independently.
- **CAD 1,000 in one go** is a large, unusual amount to be asked for in this form.

If someone contacted you about a fine, don't reply to them and don't buy anything. Check the claim directly with the organisation using a number or website you look up yourself — not one they gave you.

If you think you've already shared codes or been pressured, tell me and I'll lock your payments right away. You can also report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

- **Pressure to "move 3000 CAD in"** — urgency and a specific lump sum are standard tactics.

Real investments don't promise fixed returns, and no regulated adviser would offer this. If someone sent you this offer, don't reply, don't send money, and consider reporting it.
